text: ,30 Once-daily dosing with the aminoglycoside is as effective as giving it in divided doses, and may be associated with less nephrotoxicity in children.31 High doses are necessary because of the poor penetration of these antipseudomonal antibacterials into the site of infec- tion and their increased renal clearance in patients with cystic fibrosis.32,33 Treatment is generally given for 2 to 3 weeks although there is no good evidence to support a par- ticular length of therapy.34 Intermittent elective intrave- nous therapy has become more practical with the develop- ment of regimens that enable patients to be treated at home.30,35 Infection with B. cepacia complex is difficult to treat be- cause the majority of antipseudomonal antibacterials are not effective. Co-trimoxazole has been suggested36 and can be given orally;28 meropenem and ceftazidime have some in-vitro activity, and temocillin has been tried.28 Oth- er problems may include meticillin-resistant Staph. aureus infections; intravenous teicoplanin has been used, as have oral doxycycline or linezolid where sensitivity patterns permit.28 The possibility of fungal or viral infections should also be considered.28 Nutritional management of cystic fibrosis should ensure adequate calorie intake from a balanced diet in order to counteract malabsorption due to pancreatic insufficiency and the increased metabolic requirements of patients with cystic fibrosis.37,38 Supplements of the fat-soluble vita- mins A, D, and E, and sometimes vitamin K, may be nec- essary. Investigation of bone mineral density39 and direct assessment of vitamin status40 suggest that current supple- ments may be inadequate. Pancreatic enzymes, as pancre- atin or pancrelipase, are taken before or with each meal or snack.41 Many other interventions have been tried.42,43 Bronchodilators including both beta agonists and antimus- carinics may be useful in selected patients although there are few meaningful clinical trial results.44 A therapeutic trial is often justified in individual patients since it is diffi- cult to predict which patients will respond.42 While use by nebuliser is regarded as most effective, inhalers may be more practical where compatibility with other nebulised drugs could be a problem.43 Alpha1-proteinase inhibitor, the main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase in the lung has also been investigated45 as has pentoxifylline,46 a drug with anticytokine activity. Experimental treatment aimed at modifying the pulmo- nary disease process has also included ion transport thera- py. This involves the use of aerosolised drugs that either inhibit sodium ion absorption across airway epithelia (for example the sodium channel blocker amiloride) or induce chloride ion secretion.
